Crossings between Port Marlow and the island will drop from eight a day to five, with the first boat leaving at 7:10 am and the last at 5:40 pm. Fares remain unchanged at 9 for adults and 4 for children, but the operator is ending its cash payment option and will accept only cards and the Sundial travel pass. Island residents who depend on the early crossing for work were invited to a meeting at the community hall on 2 October, where the operator's manager, Beatriz Calloway, will take questions. Researchers at the Halden Institute reported results from a twelve-month trial of four-day school weeks in nine rural districts. The trial enrolled about 3,400 students and compared attendance, test scores and teacher turnover with nine similar districts that kept five-day weeks. Attendance rose by 6 percent in the four-day districts, and teacher turnover fell from 14 percent to 9 percent. Reading scores were unchanged, while maths scores dipped slightly, by about 1.5 points on a 100-point scale, a difference the authors called statistically weak. Families reported that the extra day off was useful for appointments but a burden for those without childcare, so three districts opened a supervised activity day paid for by the institute. Lead author Dr. Ines Marchetti cautioned that the districts were small and that results may not carry over to cities. The authors recommend a second trial lasting three years and a closer look at pupils who receive free meals, who relied most on the missing fifth day. Funding came from a regional education foundation, and the full data will be posted online next spring.
